claim: Streptococcus pneumoniae is a major pathogen in children, elderly subjects, and immunodeficient patients.
source: Streptococcus pneumoniae is a major pathogen in children, elderly subjects, and immunodeficient patients.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about S. pneumoniae as a pathogen.

claim: PTX3 is a fluid-phase pattern recognition molecule involved in resistance to selected microbial agents and in regulation of inflammation.
source: Pentraxin 3 (PTX3) is a fluid-phase pattern recognition molecule (PRM) involved in resistance to selected microbial agents and in regulation of inflammation.
evidence: This statement draws from established scientific knowledge about PTX3 function.

claim: PTX3 was strongly induced in non-hematopoietic (particularly, endothelial) cells during invasive pneumococcal infection in mice.
source: In a murine model of invasive pneumococcal infection, PTX3 was strongly induced in non-hematopoietic (particularly, endothelial) cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the murine model described in the manuscript.

claim: The IL-1β/MyD88 axis played a major role in regulation of Ptx3 gene expression during pneumococcal infection.
source: The IL-1β/MyD88 axis played a major role in regulation of the Ptx3 gene expression.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using Il1r−/− and Myd88−/− mice.

claim: Ptx3−/− mice presented more severe invasive pneumococcal infection.
source: Ptx3−/− mice presented more severe invasive pneumococcal infection.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing Ptx3−/− and WT mice.

claim: High concentrations of PTX3 had opsonic activity in vitro.
source: Although high concentrations of PTX3 had opsonic activity in vitro, no evidence of PTX3-enhanced phagocytosis was obtained in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro experimental data showing opsonic activity at high PTX3 concentrations.

claim: No evidence of PTX3-enhanced phagocytosis was obtained in vivo.
source: Although high concentrations of PTX3 had opsonic activity in vitro, no evidence of PTX3-enhanced phagocytosis was obtained in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo experimental data.

claim: Ptx3-deficient mice showed enhanced recruitment of neutrophils and inflammation.
source: In contrast, Ptx3-deficient mice showed enhanced recruitment of neutrophils and inflammation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing Ptx3−/− and WT mice.

claim: Protection against pneumococcus was dependent upon PTX3-mediated regulation of neutrophil inflammation.
source: Using P-selectin-deficient mice, we found that protection against pneumococcus was dependent upon PTX3-mediated regulation of neutrophil inflammation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using P-selectin-deficient mice.

claim: PTX3 gene polymorphisms were associated with invasive pneumococcal infections in humans.
source: In humans, PTX3 gene polymorphisms were associated with invasive pneumococcal infections.
evidence: This is supported by genetic association data from human patients.

claim: PTX3 plays an important role in tuning inflammation and resistance against invasive pneumococcal infection.
source: Thus, this fluid-phase PRM plays an important role in tuning inflammation and resistance against invasive pneumococcal infection.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Pneumococcal invasive infection occurs when pneumococcus invades the lower respiratory tract and translocates through the bloodstream into the systemic compartment.
source: Depending on the virulence factors expressed by the pathogen and on host factors, the disease can evolve to pneumococcal invasive infection, where pneumococcus invades the lower respiratory tract and translocates through the bloodstream into the systemic compartment (Weiser et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Weiser et al., 2018.

claim: PTX3 is expressed by various hematopoietic and non-hematopoietic cells in response to microbial moieties and inflammatory cytokines (i.e IL-1β and TNF).
source: PTX3 is expressed by various hematopoietic and non-hematopoietic cells in response to microbial moieties and inflammatory cytokines (i.e IL-1β and TNF), and it has been associated with the control of various infections by promoting different anti-microbial mechanisms.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about PTX3 expression.

claim: PTX3 participates directly to the elimination of selected microorganisms by promoting phagocytosis, activating the complement cascade and as a component of Neutrophil Extracellular Traps (NET).
source: Indeed, PTX3 participates directly to the elimination of selected microorganisms by promoting phagocytosis, activating the complement cascade and as a component of Neutrophil Extracellular Traps (NET) (Daigo et al., 2012; Jaillon et al., 2014; Jaillon et al., 2007; Moalli et al., 2010; Porte et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: PTX3 modulates tissue remodeling.
source: Furthermore PTX3 modulates tissue remodeling (Doni et al., 2015) and inflammation by tuning complement activation and P-selectin-dependent transmigration (Deban et al., 2010; Lech et al., 2013), both involved in neutrophil recruitment and in the evolution of respiratory tract infections (Quinton and Mizgerd, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Doni et al., 2015.

claim: PTX3 modulates inflammation by tuning complement activation and P-selectin-dependent transmigration.
source: Furthermore PTX3 modulates tissue remodeling (Doni et al., 2015) and inflammation by tuning complement activation and P-selectin-dependent transmigration (Deban et al., 2010; Lech et al., 2013), both involved in neutrophil recruitment and in the evolution of respiratory tract infections (Quinton and Mizgerd, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Deban et al., 2010 and Lech et al., 2013.

claim: PTX3 plasma levels increase in humans in the context of inflammation and selected infectious diseases, including pneumococcal pathologies.
source: In humans, PTX3 plasma levels increase in the context of inflammation and selected infectious diseases, including pneumococcal pathologies (i.e. community-acquired pneumonia, ventilator-associated pneumonia, pneumococcal exacerbated chronic obstructive pulmonary disease), correlating with the severity of the disease and predicting the risk of mortality (Bilgin et al., 2018; Kao et al., 2013; Mauri et al., 2014; Porte et al., 2019; Saleh et al., 2019; Shi et al., 2020; Siljan et al., 2019; Thulborn et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to clinical studies.

claim: PTX3 plasma levels correlate with the severity of pneumococcal disease and predict the risk of mortality.
source: In humans, PTX3 plasma levels increase in the context of inflammation and selected infectious diseases, including pneumococcal pathologies (i.e. community-acquired pneumonia, ventilator-associated pneumonia, pneumococcal exacerbated chronic obstructive pulmonary disease), correlating with the severity of the disease and predicting the risk of mortality (Bilgin et al., 2018; Kao et al., 2013; Mauri et al., 2014; Porte et al., 2019; Saleh et al., 2019; Shi et al., 2020; Siljan et al., 2019; Thulborn et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to clinical studies.

claim: Single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in the PTX3 gene have been associated with patient susceptibility to respiratory infections.
source: In addition, single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in the PTX3 gene have been associated with patient susceptibility to respiratory infections (Brunel et al., 2018; Chiarini et al., 2010; Cunha et al., 2015; Cunha et al., 2014; He et al., 2018; Olesen et al., 2007; Wójtowicz et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to genetic association studies.

claim: S. pneumoniae serotype 3 causes bacterial colonization of the respiratory tract, then disseminates through the blood circulation and infects other organs like the spleen, resulting in death within 3–4 days.
source: As already described, S. pneumoniae serotype 3 causes bacterial colonization of the respiratory tract, then disseminates through the blood circulation and infects other organs like the spleen, resulting in death within 3–4 days (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A ,B; de Porto et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B and a citation to de Porto et al., 2019.

claim: Infected mice developed organ dysfunction, as demonstrated by increased circulating levels of creatinine and enzymatic activity of alanine transaminase and creatine phosphokinase 36 hr post-infection.
source: When compared to uninfected mice, infected animals also developed organ dysfunction, as demonstrated by increased circulating levels of creatinine and enzymatic activity of alanine transaminase and creatine phosphokinase 36 hr post-infection (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: PTX3 expression was detected in the alveolar compartment near the pulmonary veins as early as 6 hr post-infection.
source: As early as 6 hr post-infection, we detected a local expression of PTX3 in the alveolar compartment near the pulmonary veins (Figure 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 1A, B.

claim: PTX3 staining was detected in endothelial cells in the area where inflammatory cells infiltration was observed at 12 hr post-infection.
source: At 12 hr post-infection, we were able to detect PTX3-specific staining in endothelial cells in the area where we can appreciate inflammatory cells infiltration.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data.

claim: Strong PTX3 staining was present near the recruitment site of inflammatory cells forming inflammatory foci at 24 hr post-infection.
source: This association was confirmed 24 hr post-infection, when a strong PTX3 staining was present near the recruitment site of inflammatory cells forming inflammatory foci (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Local and systemic production of PTX3 was strongly induced by the infection during the disseminating phase.
source: Interestingly, local and systemic production of PTX3 was strongly induced by the infection during the disseminating phase (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Ptx3 was upregulated mainly in the lung, aorta, and heart during invasive infection.
source: During this invasive infection we observed that Ptx3 was upregulated mainly in the lung, aorta, and heart, while other organs like brain, kidneys, and liver did not show higher Ptx3 expression compared to the uninfected mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: A rapid induction of IL-1β was observed in the pneumococcal invasive infection model.
source: In this pneumococcal invasive infection model we observed a rapid induction of IL-1β (Figure 2A), and a strong correlation between the levels of IL-1β expressed in the respiratory tract with the levels of lung PTX3 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: There is a strong correlation between the levels of IL-1β expressed in the respiratory tract with the levels of lung PTX3.
source: In this pneumococcal invasive infection model we observed a rapid induction of IL-1β (Figure 2A), and a strong correlation between the levels of IL-1β expressed in the respiratory tract with the levels of lung PTX3 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A similar correlation was observed with TNF and IL-6 levels measured in homogenates from infected lungs.
source: A similar correlation was observed with TNF and IL-6 levels measured in homogenates from infected lungs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B), whereas CXCR1 levels were not correlated with the level of lung PTX3 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: CXCR1 levels were not correlated with the level of lung PTX3.
source: A similar correlation was observed with TNF and IL-6 levels measured in homogenates from infected lungs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B), whereas CXCR1 levels were not correlated with the level of lung PTX3 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Il1r−/− mice infected by S. pneumoniae showed lower PTX3 levels, locally and systemically.
source: Moreover, Il1r−/− mice infected by S. pneumoniae showed lower PTX3 levels, locally and systemically (i.e. in the lung and the serum, respectively) (Figure 2C, D).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2C, D.

claim: Myd88−/− mice infected with S. pneumoniae were not able to produce PTX3 in the lung.
source: S. pneumoniae infected Myd88−/− mice were not able to produce PTX3 in the lung and presented the same impairment of PTX3 production as Il1r−/− mice (Figure 2C, D).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2C, D.

claim: PTX3 production during pneumococcal infection requires IL-1β sensing or contribution of MyD88-dependent pathways.
source: These data suggest that, similar to what occurs in other models, PTX3 production during pneumococcal infection requires IL-1β sensing or contribution of MyD88-dependent pathways (Doni et al., 2015; Jaillon et al., 2014; Salio et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data with Il1r−/− and Myd88−/− mice, supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Human neutrophils can release PTX3 upon stimulation with S. pneumoniae.
source: In agreement, we observed that human neutrophils can release PTX3 upon stimulation with S. pneumoniae (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Csf3r−/− mice are characterized by chronic neutropenia, granulocyte, and macrophage progenitor cell deficiency and impaired neutrophil mobilization.
source: These mice are characterized by chronic neutropenia, granulocyte, and macrophage progenitor cell deficiency and impaired neutrophil mobilization (Liu et al., 1996; Ponzetta et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Liu et al., 1996 and Ponzetta et al., 2019.

claim: Csf3r−/− mice presented lower levels of myeloperoxidase (MPO) in lung homogenates at 36 hr post-infection.
source: Following pneumococcal infection, Csf3r−/− mice presented lower levels of myeloperoxidase (MPO), a marker of neutrophil recruitment, in lung homogenates at 36 hr post-infection (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Csf3r−/− mice expressed the same pulmonary levels of PTX3 as WT mice despite having lower neutrophil recruitment.
source: By contrast, even though these mice presented lower amount of neutrophils recruited in response to the infection, they expressed the same pulmonary levels of PTX3 as WT mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Neutrophils are not the main source of PTX3 in the murine model of pneumococcal invasive infection.
source: These results suggest that neutrophils are not the main source of PTX3 in our murine model of pneumococcal invasive infection.
evidence: This is an inference from the Csf3r−/− mouse data.

claim: PTX3 is mainly produced by the non-hematopoietic compartment after pneumococcal infection.
source: During pneumococcal infection, we did not observe any difference in the levels of PTX3 in the respiratory tract and in the serum of WT mice receiving bone marrow from Ptx3−/− or WT animals, while no PTX3 was measured in Ptx3−/− mice receiving WT or Ptx3−/− bone marrow (Figure 3A, B). These results suggest that PTX3 is mainly produced by the non-hematopoietic compartment after pneumococcal infection.
evidence: This is supported by bone marrow chimera data shown in Figure 3A, B.

claim: Endothelial cells are an important source of PTX3.
source: Endothelial cells were described as an important source of PTX3 (Garlanda et al., 2018), thus we evaluated their contribution to PTX3 production during pneumococcal infection.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Garlanda et al., 2018.

claim: Ptx3Lox/LoxCdh5Cre/+ mice presented approximately 50% reduction of PTX3 levels compared to PTX3-competent mice when infected with S. pneumoniae.
source: When Ptx3Lox/LoxCdh5Cre/+ mice were infected with S. pneumoniae, they presented approximately 50% reduction of PTX3 levels compared to PTX3-competent mice (Figure 3C, D).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3C, D.

claim: Both murine and human endothelial cells can produce PTX3 after stimulation with S. pneumoniae.
source: In vitro experiments confirmed the ability of both murine and human endothelial cells to produce PTX3 after stimulation with S. pneumoniae (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Non-hematopoietic cells, mainly endothelial cells, are a major source of PTX3 in the pneumococcal infection model.
source: Thus, in our setting, non-hematopoietic cells, mainly endothelial cells, are a major source of PTX3.
evidence: This is an inference from the bone marrow chimera and conditional knockout data.

claim: A significant increase of the bacterial load in the lung was observed in Ptx3−/− mice during the invasive phase of infection (i.e. 36 hr post-infection), compared to WT mice.
source: When Ptx3−/− mice were infected with S. pneumoniae (5 × 104 CFU), a significant increase of the bacterial load in the lung was observed during the invasive phase of infection (i.e. 36 hr post-infection), compared to WT mice (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by bacterial load data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Defective local control of bacterial growth in Ptx3−/− mice was associated to an increase of bacterial load in the spleen.
source: Defective local control of bacterial growth was associated to an increase of bacterial load in the spleen (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by bacterial load data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: There was no difference in bacterial load between WT and Ptx3−/− mice at earlier time points (i.e. 18 hr post-infection).
source: Interestingly there was no difference at earlier time points (i.e. 18 hr post-infection, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that PTX3 exerted a role in the control of pneumococcal infection mainly during the invasive phase.
evidence: This is supported by bacterial load data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: PTX3 exerted a role in the control of pneumococcal infection mainly during the invasive phase.
source: Interestingly there was no difference at earlier time points (i.e. 18 hr post-infection, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that PTX3 exerted a role in the control of pneumococcal infection mainly during the invasive phase.
evidence: This is an inference from the time-course bacterial load data.

claim: Ptx3−/− mice showed a significant higher mortality (83.3%) compared to WT animals (around 30%) when infected with 5 × 103 CFU of S. pneumoniae serotype 3.
source: Using a bacterial dose (5 × 103 CFU) inducing around 30% mortality in WT animals, Ptx3−/− mice showed a significant higher mortality (83.3%; p < 0.001) (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Strong PTX3 production was observed during the invasive phase of infection with S. pneumoniae serotype 1.
source: In fact, when mice were infected with S. pneumoniae serotype 1, we observed a strong PTX3 production during the invasive phase of the infection (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) and a correlation with IL-1β levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: PTX3 production correlated with IL-1β levels during S. pneumoniae serotype 1 infection.
source: In fact, when mice were infected with S. pneumoniae serotype 1, we observed a strong PTX3 production during the invasive phase of the infection (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) and a correlation with IL-1β levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Ptx3−/− mice infected by serotype 1 presented a higher number of bacteria at the local site of infection and also in the spleen 24 hr post-infection compared to WT animals.
source: Ptx3−/− mice infected by serotype 1 presented a higher sensitivity to the infection compared to WT animals, with a higher number of bacteria at the local site of infection and also in the spleen 24 hr post-infection (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: This is supported by bacterial load data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, E.

claim: The protection conferred by PTX3 is not limited to serotype 3, and embraces other bacterial serotypes of clinical relevance, including serotype 1.
source: Thus, in the applied model of S. pneumoniae infection, the protection conferred by PTX3 is not limited to serotype 3, and embraces other bacterial serotypes of clinical relevance, including serotype 1.
evidence: This is an inference from the data with both serotype 3 and serotype 1.

claim: Systemic administration of recombinant PTX3 to Ptx3−/− mice rescues the phenotype.
source: Systemic administration of recombinant PTX3 to Ptx3−/− mice rescues the phenotype. As reported in Figure 4D, PTX3 administration in Ptx3−/− mice reduced lung colonization to the same level observed in WT mice.
evidence: This is supported by bacterial load data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Local treatment with 1 µg of recombinant PTX3 before infection reduced pulmonary bacterial load by 44% compared to vehicle-treated mice.
source: WT animals were treated locally with 1 µg of recombinant protein before infection or 12 hr post-infection. Under both conditions we observed a significant reduction (44% and 57%, respectively; p < 0.01) of the pulmonary bacterial load compared with the CFU found in mice treated with vehicle alone (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by bacterial load data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Local treatment with 1 µg of recombinant PTX3 12 hr post-infection reduced pulmonary bacterial load by 57% compared to vehicle-treated mice.
source: WT animals were treated locally with 1 µg of recombinant protein before infection or 12 hr post-infection. Under both conditions we observed a significant reduction (44% and 57%, respectively; p < 0.01) of the pulmonary bacterial load compared with the CFU found in mice treated with vehicle alone (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by bacterial load data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The incubation of S. pneumoniae with 25–250 µg/ml of recombinant PTX3 did not have any effect on the growth rate of the bacteria.
source: The incubation of S. pneumoniae with 25–250 µg/ml of recombinant PTX3 did not have any effect on the growth rate of the bacteria (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro growth assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: PTX3 binding to S. pneumoniae serotype 3 was not observed at physiological concentrations (106 CFU/100 ng PTX3).
source: By using a flow cytometry assay, we analyzed PTX3 binding to S. pneumoniae serotype 3 mimicking the bacteria/PTX3 ratio found in the infected lung (106 CFU/100 ng PTX3). Under these conditions, we did not observe any interaction of PTX3 with bacteria and, even with an amount of PTX3 5- to 10-fold higher than the one produced in the entire lung, less than 1% of the bacteria were bound (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry binding data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: At 500 µg/ml of PTX3, binding to only 36.4% of S. pneumoniae serotype 3 bacteria was observed.
source: At 500 µg/ml of PTX3 (5000-fold higher than in the lung homogenates) we observed binding to only 36.4% of bacteria (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry binding data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: PTX3 exerts opsonic effects, increasing the phagocytosis of pneumococcus by human neutrophils, but only at very high concentrations (higher than 100 µg/ml).
source: In a first set of experiments, human neutrophils were incubated with PTX3-opsonized S. pneumoniae-GFP. We confirmed that PTX3 exerts opsonic effects, increasing the phagocytosis of pneumococcus by neutrophils, but only at very high concentrations, that is higher than 100 µg/ml (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro phagocytosis data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Mice infected with PTX3-opsonized S. pneumoniae serotype 3 showed the same local bacterial burden at 6–36 hr after infection as mice infected with pneumococcus incubated with PBS.
source: Mice infected with PTX3-opsonized S. pneumoniae serotype 3 showed the same local bacterial burden at 6–36 hr after infection as mice infected with pneumococcus incubated with PBS (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo bacterial load data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: No difference was observed in the percentage of neutrophils phagocytizing S. pneumoniae-GFP in the BAL or in the lung between WT and Ptx3-deficient mice.
source: Interestingly, we did not observe any difference in the percentage of neutrophils phagocytizing S. pneumoniae-GFP in the BAL or in the lung (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry phagocytosis data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: No difference was observed in the killing ability of neutrophils collected from WT and Ptx3-deficient mice.
source: Finally, we assessed the killing ability of neutrophils collected from WT and Ptx3-deficient mice. We did not observe any difference in the percentage of S. pneumoniae serotype 3 killed by purified murine neutrophils neither after 1 hr of incubation (WT: 79.02 ± 2.87 and Ptx3−/−: 80.48 ± 2.87, p = 0.15) or 3 hr of incubation when nearly all pneumococcus were efficiently killed (WT: 99.46 ± 0.30 and Ptx3−/−: 96.55 ± 5.40, p = 0.31) (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro killing assay data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The role of PTX3 in resistance to invasive pneumococcus infection is not accounted for by its opsonic activity.
source: These results suggest that the role of PTX3 in resistance to invasive pneumococcus infection is not accounted for by its opsonic activity.
evidence: This is an inference from the phagocytosis and killing data.

claim: Pneumococcal invasive disease induced by S. pneumoniae serotype 3 was characterized by a multifocal neutrophilic bronchopneumonia.
source: In pneumococcal invasive disease induced by S. pneumoniae serotype 3, infection was characterized by a multifocal neutrophilic bronchopneumonia (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The main inflammatory cell recruitment was observed during the invasive phase of the infection (starting from 24 hr after infection).
source: The main inflammatory cell recruitment was observed during the invasive phase of the infection (starting from 24 hr after infection), when the pulmonary MPO was dramatically increased (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by MPO data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: An initial recruitment of neutrophils, characterized by an increased number of neutrophils both in the BAL and in the lung parenchyma, was observed during the first 6 hr of infection.
source: We analyzed more accurately neutrophil recruitment in the lung and in the BAL of infected mice and we observed two phases of neutrophil recruitment. An initial recruitment, characterized by an increased (i.e. threefold compared to uninfected lung) number of neutrophils both in the BAL and in the lung parenchyma, was observed during the first 6 hr of infection.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data.

claim: In the next 12–24 hr of infection, an important recruitment of neutrophils in the lung (i.e. 4-fold compared to uninfected lung) that translocated into the alveolar space (up to 50-fold compared to uninfected BAL) was observed.
source: In the next 12–24 hr of infection we observed an important recruitment of neutrophils in the lung (i.e. 4-fold compared to uninfected lung) that translocated into the alveolar space (up to 50-fold compared to uninfected BAL) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: The first phase of neutrophil recruitment is important for the early control of the infection, reducing the number of colonizing bacteria.
source: These two steps of recruitment have been described to exert opposite roles (Bou Ghanem et al., 2015). Indeed, the first phase is important for the early control of the infection, reducing the number of colonizing bacteria.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bou Ghanem et al., 2015.

claim: The second phase of neutrophil recruitment has been associated with the development of the inflammatory environment, leading to tissue damage that could promote growth and invasion of the bacteria.
source: In contrast the second phase has been associated with the development of the inflammatory environment, leading to tissue damage that could promote growth and invasion of the bacteria (Bou Ghanem et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bou Ghanem et al., 2015.

claim: The inflammatory profile was significantly increased in Ptx3−/− mice at 18 hr after infection, as shown by an increased development of foci in the lung induced by a higher inflammatory cell recruitment.
source: Interestingly, the inflammatory profile was significantly increased in Ptx3−/− mice, as shown by an increased development of foci in the lung induced by a higher inflammatory cell recruitment (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 6A–C.

claim: Ptx3−/− mice had a quicker and more severe formation of inflammatory foci compared to the WT.
source: Moreover, looking at the time course of the development of pneumococcal-induced respiratory inflammation, we observed that Ptx3−/− mice had a quicker and more severe formation of inflammatory foci compared to the WT (Figure 6B, C).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 6B, C.

claim: Ptx3−/− mice presented an increased vascular damage score based on higher perivascular edema and hemorrhages.
source: Furthermore, these mice presented also an increased vascular damage score based on higher perivascular edema and hemorrhages (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by histological scoring data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The higher inflammation in Ptx3-deficient mice was due to a significant increase of neutrophil recruitment in the BAL and the lung.
source: Flow cytometry analysis revealed that the higher inflammation in Ptx3-deficient mice was due to a significant increase of neutrophil recruitment in the BAL and the lung (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: No change was observed in the recruitment of other myeloid cells, namely macrophages, eosinophils, and monocytes in Ptx3-deficient mice.
source: Moreover, we did not observe any change in the recruitment of other myeloid cells, namely macrophages, eosinophils, and monocytes.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data.

claim: The increased neutrophil recruitment phenotype in Ptx3-deficient mice was also observed with the serotype 1 model of invasive pneumococcal infection.
source: This phenotype was also observed with the serotype 1 model of invasive pneumococcal infection (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Intranasal treatment with recombinant PTX3 was associated with a decrease in the neutrophil number in BAL and lungs.
source: Finally, we observed that intranasal treatment with recombinant PTX3 was also associated with a decrease in the neutrophil number in BAL and lungs, demonstrating that PTX3 has a direct role in the control of neutrophil migration in the respiratory tract (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: PTX3 has a direct role in the control of neutrophil migration in the respiratory tract.
source: Finally, we observed that intranasal treatment with recombinant PTX3 was also associated with a decrease in the neutrophil number in BAL and lungs, demonstrating that PTX3 has a direct role in the control of neutrophil migration in the respiratory tract (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is an inference from the PTX3 treatment data.

claim: Neutrophil depletion during the invasive phase resulted in protection against pneumococcal infection.
source: It has been shown that neutrophil depletion during the invasive phase resulted in protection against pneumococcal infection (Bou Ghanem et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bou Ghanem et al., 2015.

claim: Treatment with anti-Ly6G significantly reduced neutrophils infiltration in the lungs of WT mice infected intranasally with S. pneumoniae.
source: In WT mice infected intranasally with S. pneumoniae, treatment with anti-Ly6G significantly reduced neutrophils infiltration in the lungs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Treatment with anti-Ly6G completely abolished the increased accumulation of neutrophils observed in Ptx3−/− mice.
source: In addition, treatment with anti-Ly6G completely abolished the increased accumulation of neutrophils observed in Ptx3−/− mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: The reduction of neutrophil recruitment in both WT and Ptx3−/− mice treated with anti-Ly6G resulted in a significant reduction of the local and systemic bacterial load.
source: The reduction of neutrophil recruitment in both WT and Ptx3−/− mice treated with anti-Ly6G resulted in a significant reduction of the local and systemic bacterial load, compared to mice treated with the isotype control (Figure 7A, B).
evidence: This is supported by bacterial load data shown in Figure 7A, B.

claim: Ptx3−/− mice treated with neutrophil depleting antibody were not more infected than the WT mice.
source: In addition, Ptx3−/− mice treated with neutrophil depleting antibody were not more infected than the WT mice (Figure 7A, B).
evidence: This is supported by bacterial load data shown in Figure 7A, B.

claim: Taming of pneumococcus-promoting neutrophil recruitment underlies the role of PTX3 in resistance against this bacterial pathogen.
source: These results suggest that taming of pneumococcus-promoting neutrophil recruitment underlies the role of PTX3 in resistance against this bacterial pathogen.
evidence: This is an inference from the neutrophil depletion data.

claim: No differences were detected in the levels of CXCL1 and CXCL2 between Ptx3-deficient and WT mice at 18 hr post-infection.
source: At 18 hr post-infection, even though there was a higher amount of neutrophils in the airways of Ptx3−/− mice, we did not detect any differences in the levels of CXCL1 and CXCL2 between Ptx3-deficient and WT mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: No difference in the levels of the potent chemoattractants C3a and C5a was observed between Ptx3-deficient and WT mice.
source: Since PTX3 is a well-known regulator of complement activation (Haapasalo and Meri, 2019), we investigated the levels of the two anaphylatoxins C3a and C5a in the lung homogenates of infected mice. No difference in the levels of the potent chemoattractants C3a and C5a, was observed (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The levels of C3d were similar in Ptx3-deficient and WT mice.
source: The levels of C3d, a C3 degradation product deposited on the surface of cells and a marker of complement activation in lung homogenates, were similar in Ptx3-deficient and WT mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: No difference in P-selectin levels was observed both in WT and Ptx3-deficient mice at steady state and after S. pneumoniae infection.
source: We first evaluated P-selectin levels in lungs at steady state and after S. pneumoniae infection, excluding the presence of any difference in P-selectin levels both in WT and Ptx3-deficient mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1E.

claim: PTX3 could block 40% of the neutrophil migration induced by S. pneumoniae in vitro.
source: We investigated the ability of PTX3 to dampen neutrophil transmigration through endothelial cell layer in vitro, using S. pneumoniae as the attractive signal. We observed that PTX3 could block 40% of the neutrophil migration induced by S. pneumoniae (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro transmigration assay data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Treatment of endothelial cells with anti-CD62P (anti-P-selectin) antibody induced the same blocking effect on neutrophil migration as PTX3.
source: Moreover, treatment of endothelial cells with anti-CD62P (anti-P-selectin) antibody induced the same blocking effect. We did not observe any additional blocking effect of PTX3 in association with anti-CD62P, suggesting that PTX3 exerts its blocking effect through P-selectin.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro transmigration assay data.

claim: PTX3 exerts its blocking effect on neutrophil migration through P-selectin.
source: Moreover, treatment of endothelial cells with anti-CD62P (anti-P-selectin) antibody induced the same blocking effect. We did not observe any additional blocking effect of PTX3 in association with anti-CD62P, suggesting that PTX3 exerts its blocking effect through P-selectin.
evidence: This is an inference from the in vitro transmigration assay data.

claim: In Selp−/− mice, PTX3 treatment did not reduce the bacterial load.
source: To confirm that PTX3 protects infected mice by blocking P-selectin, we used P-selectin-deficient mice (Selp−/−). In Selp−/− mice PTX3 treatment did not reduce the bacterial load (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by bacterial load data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Anti-CD62P treatment completely abolished the higher neutrophils recruitment in Ptx3-deficient mice.
source: Moreover, we treated WT and Ptx3-deficient mice with anti-CD62P, to block P-selectin-dependent neutrophil transmigration during the invasive phase of infection. Anti-CD62P treatment completely abolished the higher neutrophils recruitment in Ptx3-deficient mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F, G).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1F, G.

claim: The higher neutrophil infiltration observed during pneumococcal pneumonia in the absence of PTX3 is dependent on P-selectin.
source: This result suggests that the higher neutrophil infiltration observed during pneumococcal pneumonia in the absence of PTX3 is dependent on P-selectin.
evidence: This is an inference from the anti-CD62P treatment data.

claim: The reduction of neutrophil recruitment in Ptx3-deficient mice treated with anti-CD62P is associated with a significant reduction of the local and systemic bacterial load reaching the same level observed in WT mice treated with anti-CD62P.
source: Importantly, the reduction of neutrophil recruitment in Ptx3-deficient mice treated with anti-CD62P is associated with a significant reduction of the local and systemic bacterial load reaching the same level observed in WT mice treated with anti-CD62P (Figure 7E, F).
evidence: This is supported by bacterial load data shown in Figure 7E, F.

claim: Genetic deficiency in P-selectin and PTX3 completely rescued the phenotype observed in Ptx3−/− mice.
source: Finally, to assess the role of the P-selectin pathway in PTX3-mediated resistance against invasive pneumococcus infection, we took advantage of Ptx3−/−Selp−/− double deficient mice. As shown in Figure 7G, H, genetic deficiency in P-selectin and PTX3 completely rescued the phenotype observed in Ptx3−/− mice.
evidence: This is supported by bacterial load data shown in Figure 7G, H.

claim: The defective control of invasive pneumococcal infection observed in Ptx3−/− mice is due to unleashing P-selectin-dependent recruitment of pneumococcus-promoting neutrophils.
source: Thus, the defective control of invasive pneumococcal infection observed in Ptx3−/− mice is due to unleashing P-selectin-dependent recruitment of pneumococcus-promoting neutrophils.
evidence: This is an inference from the double knockout mouse data.

claim: The AAA haplotype was twice as frequent in IPD patients as in healthy controls (9.67% and 4.26%, respectively, p = 0.0102).
source: However, when the haplotypes determined by the three SNPs (rs2305619, rs3816527, and rs1840680) were examined, we found that the AAA haplotype was twice as frequent in IPD patients as in healthy controls (9.67% and 4.26%, respectively, p = 0.0102, Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by genetic association data shown in Table 2.

claim: No significant associations were observed between haplotypes and severity of the disease, evaluated as number of patients developing bacteremia or sepsis.
source: Nevertheless, no significant associations were observed between haplotypes and severity of the disease, evaluated as number of patients developing bacteremia or sepsis (Table 3).
evidence: This is supported by genetic association data shown in Table 3.

claim: The +734A allele was associated in various studies with decreased PTX3 circulating levels.
source: In addition, the +734A allele was associated in various studies with decreased PTX3 circulating levels (Barbati et al., 2012; Bonacina et al., 2019; Cunha et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Barbati et al., 2012, Bonacina et al., 2019, and Cunha et al., 2014.

claim: The two PTX3 protein variants (D48 and A48) had almost identical electrophoretic mobilities when run on denaturing gels both in reducing and non-reducing conditions.
source: These two proteins had almost identical electrophoretic mobilities when run on denaturing gels both in reducing and non-reducing conditions (Figure 8A), where they showed a pattern of bands consistent with previous studies (Inforzato et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by gel electrophoresis data shown in Figure 8A and a citation to Inforzato et al., 2008.

claim: Similar chromatograms were recorded when the D48 and A48 variants were resolved on a size exclusion chromatography (SEC) column in native conditions.
source: Also, similar chromatograms were recorded when the D48 and A48 variants were resolved on a size exclusion chromatography (SEC) column in native conditions (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by SEC data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The +734A/C polymorphism does not affect structure and composition of the PTX3 oligosaccharides, with major regard to their terminal residues of sialic acid.
source: Given that protein glycosylation is a major determinant of the interaction of PTX3 with P-selectin (Deban et al., 2010), it is worth pointing out that the +734A/C polymorphism does not affect structure and composition of the PTX3 oligosaccharides, with major regard to their terminal residues of sialic acid (Bally et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Deban et al., 2010 and Bally et al., 2019.

claim: The two PTX3 protein variants (D48 and A48) equally bound plastic-immobilized P-selectin.
source: In this regard, when assayed in solid phase binding experiments, these two proteins equally bound plastic-immobilized P-selectin (Figure 8C), and C1q (Figure 8D, here used as a control), indicating that the +734A/C polymorphism (i.e. the D/A amino acid substitution at position 48 of the PTX3 preprotein) does not affect the interaction of this PRM with P-selectin.
evidence: This is supported by binding assay data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The +734A/C polymorphism does not affect the interaction of PTX3 with P-selectin.
source: In this regard, when assayed in solid phase binding experiments, these two proteins equally bound plastic-immobilized P-selectin (Figure 8C), and C1q (Figure 8D, here used as a control), indicating that the +734A/C polymorphism (i.e. the D/A amino acid substitution at position 48 of the PTX3 preprotein) does not affect the interaction of this PRM with P-selectin.
evidence: This is an inference from the binding assay data.

claim: The +734A/C SNP determines reduced expression rather than function of the PTX3 protein in vivo.
source: It is therefore conceivable that the +734A/C SNP (and the others investigated in our association study) determines reduced expression rather than function of the PTX3 protein in vivo, as observed in other opportunistic infections (Cunha et al., 2014).
evidence: This is speculation based on the binding data and supported by a citation to Cunha et al., 2014.

claim: PTX3 genetic deficiency was associated with higher inflammation and disease severity in invasive pneumococcal infection.
source: In a well-characterized murine model of S. pneumoniae infection, PTX3 expression was rapidly upregulated in the alveolar and bronchiolar compartments of the lungs as well as in serum. Genetic deficiency of PTX3 was associated with higher inflammation and disease severity, as also indicated by the analysis of PTX3 genetic variants in a cohort of IPD patients.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the murine model and human genetic association data.

claim: PTX3 effect was independent from opsonophagocytosis and complement activation.
source: PTX3 effect was independent from opsonophagocytosis and complement activation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing no effect on phagocytosis or complement activation.

claim: Neutrophil recruitment through interaction with P-selectin was mainly responsible for regulation of tissue damage and pneumococcal systemic dissemination.
source: Neutrophil recruitment through interaction with P-selectin was mainly responsible for regulation of tissue damage and pneumococcal systemic dissemination.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data with P-selectin-deficient mice and anti-CD62P treatment.

claim: PTX3 plays a non-redundant role in the control of S. pneumoniae infection, modulating neutrophil-associated respiratory tissue damage and pneumococcal systemic dissemination.
source: Hence, PTX3 plays a non-redundant role in the control of S. pneumoniae infection, modulating neutrophil-associated respiratory tissue damage and pneumococcal systemic dissemination.
evidence: This is an inference from all the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: By taming uncontrolled P-selectin-dependent recruitment of neutrophils, the fluid-phase PRM PTX3 plays an essential role in tuning inflammation and resistance against invasive pneumococcus infection.
source: The results reported here suggest that, by taming uncontrolled P-selectin-dependent recruitment of neutrophils, the fluid-phase PRM PTX3 plays an essential role in tuning inflammation and resistance against invasive pneumococcus infection.
evidence: This is an inference from all the experimental data presented in the study.
